## NGO Website Development in India: Will Your Donation Site Survive a Viral Appeal? Preparing for Traffic Spikes

Your donation site will survive a viral appeal only if the pages a stranger sees first are served from a cache rather than built from scratch for every visitor, the hosting plan has headroom for a sudden crowd, and you have tested that crowd before it arrives. In NGO website development in India, this is rarely about buying the biggest server. It is about deciding which few pages must never fail, making them light and cacheable, rehearsing the spike with a load test, watching the site from outside, and keeping a fallback ready so that a failure does not cost you the donor.

We quote no traffic statistics, because we cannot source a reliable one for Indian NGOs. Technical claims come from named documentation, and features change, so confirm details with your provider.

## Why donation traffic arrives in spikes

Most NGO sites have a quiet baseline: a few visitors an hour, mostly people checking your registration or reading about a programme. Giving arrives in bursts tied to a moment, and the moment is often outside your control.

- **A campaign launch.** You send a WhatsApp broadcast, an email and a social post within the same ten minutes, and everyone who will respond responds together.
- **A disaster or emergency.** People want to help immediately and look for organisations working on the ground. Attention peaks fast and fades fast.
- **Festival seasons.** Many donors give around Diwali, Eid, Christmas or other occasions that matter in their community. Dates move each year. See [festival and year-end campaign pages](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-festival-year-end-campaign-pages-2026) covers the planning side.
- **The financial year-end.** Donors who think about the tax year often act in the weeks before 31 March. We make no tax claim here, and donors should check with their own chartered accountant, but expect your January to March traffic to look different from October. Your own past analytics is the best evidence.
- **A viral share or press mention.** A well-known person shares your link or a news site covers a story.

These visitors are cold, impatient and nearly simultaneous, which breaks sites that run well on an ordinary day.

### Average load is the wrong number

A plan that serves your normal visitors can still fail when many people arrive in the same minute, because what matters is how many requests the server handles at once. k6, an open-source load testing tool, describes a spike test as one that validates "the behavior and survival of your system in cases of sudden, short, and massive increases in activity" ([Grafana k6 documentation](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/testing-guides/test-types/)). That describes a viral appeal exactly.

## NGO website development in India: where donation sites actually fail

A site rarely fails in one dramatic way. It degrades step by step, and the weakest link decides what donors see. These are the common weak links, roughly in the order they give way.

### Shared hosting limits

Low-cost shared hosting puts many sites on one server and limits what each account may use, such as CPU time, memory and simultaneous processes. The limits are usually in the provider's terms or fair-use policy. At the ceiling, visitors typically see slow pages or errors such as 503, and some providers suspend an account temporarily. See [shared, cloud and managed WordPress hosting](/blog/wordpress-hosting-shared-cloud-managed). Ask your host in writing what happens when you exceed limits.

### Uncached WordPress pages

A default WordPress page is generated on request: PHP runs, the database is queried and the HTML is assembled. That is fine for ten visitors and expensive for thousands arriving together. The WordPress developer handbook notes that caching plugins "cache your WordPress posts and pages as static files" and that this can "improve performance several hundred times over for fairly static pages" ([WordPress developer resources, optimization](https://developer.wordpress.org/advanced-administration/performance/optimization/)). A campaign page, which is mostly a story, a photo and a donate button, is exactly the "fairly static" case.

### Database and plugin load

Every plugin adds code that runs on requests, and some add database queries to every page. The WordPress guide recommends deleting unnecessary plugins and selectively disabling plugins to measure server performance, and notes that too many autoloaded options can slow a site. It adds that a persistent object cache saves trips to the database but needs your host to offer a cache server. Before a campaign, remove plugins you no longer use, find the slow ones, and ask whether an object cache is available on your plan.

Keep entry pages public and cacheable, and confine per-person work (forms, receipts, donor dashboards) to the narrow donation step.

### Payment-page timeouts

The final step usually hands the donor to, or embeds a form from, a third-party payment provider. Your server must create an order before the donor can pay, and when it is slow that step can time out even though the provider is healthy. A donor who sees a spinner and then an error will give up or try twice. Keep the code before the hand-off light, and show a donation's status when the donor returns instead of an error. This article is about capacity, so it does not cover gateway choice or charges.

### Email and SMS limits

After each donation your site probably sends a receipt email and perhaps an SMS or WhatsApp message. Email providers, SMS gateways and messaging platforms set sending limits, and these differ by provider and plan. A burst of donations can delay or drop receipts, and donors then phone to ask whether the gift worked. Read your provider's documented limits, queue messages instead of sending them inside the donation request, and show a confirmation on screen so the donor need not wait for an email.

## Caching and CDN basics, without the jargon

Caching means keeping a ready-made copy so the server does not rebuild it each time. Two layers matter most here (browser and object caching also help, as the WordPress guide notes).

| Layer | What it does | Typical NGO use |
|---|---|---|
| Page cache (on your server or by a plugin) | Stores the finished HTML of a page so PHP and the database are skipped | Campaign page, home page, story pages |
| CDN or edge cache | Copies of your files kept on servers around the world, close to visitors | Images, scripts, fonts and, if configured, the HTML of public pages |

### Page cache first

If you do one thing, serve the campaign page as a cached page. The server then does almost no work per visitor, and the same copy answers thousands of requests. Most WordPress caching plugins and many managed hosts provide this. Test it logged out, check that edits appear after you clear the cache, and confirm the donation form still works on a cached page.

### What a CDN adds

A content delivery network keeps copies of your files on servers in many locations, so visitors are served from a nearby one and your own server sees fewer requests. Cloudflare is a widely used example. Its documentation lists static types it caches by default, such as images, stylesheets, scripts and fonts, and states plainly that "the Cloudflare CDN does not cache HTML or JSON by default" ([Cloudflare, default cache behavior](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/concepts/default-cache-behavior/)). So a CDN speeds up images and scripts at once, but page HTML still comes from your server unless you create a rule. Cloudflare points to Cache Rules, which control what is eligible for caching, how long it is kept and where ([Cloudflare, Cache Rules](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/how-to/cache-rules/)).

Caching HTML at the edge suits a public campaign page and is risky for anything personal. Cache only pages identical for every visitor, keep forms, receipts and logged-in areas out, and retest after any change. Cached copies also delay your edits: decide how long the campaign page may be cached, know how to purge it, and put "purge cache" on your checklist.

### The static donation page approach

For the most important public page, consider a simple page of mostly static content: one story, a few optimised images, a clear amount selector and a button that opens the secure payment step. Nothing on it depends on the visitor, so almost any hosting setup can serve it and cache it aggressively. Our guide to [building for slow phones and weak networks](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-low-bandwidth-mobile-donors-2026) covers weight and speed for the same page. The payment step remains dynamic, and that is the part you test hardest.

## Load test before the campaign, not during it

A load test sends many simulated visitors to your site and records what happens. It tells you where the break point is while you can still fix it. You do not need to be a performance engineer to run a basic one, but you do need to be careful about where you point it.

### Know the test types

The k6 documentation distinguishes several types ([Grafana k6, test types](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/testing-guides/test-types/)). A smoke test validates that the script works under minimal load. A load test examines performance under expected normal conditions. A stress test assesses behaviour at the limits, when load exceeds the expected average. A spike test covers sudden, short, massive increases, and a soak test covers reliability over extended periods. For an NGO the useful order is smoke, then a load test at a realistic number, then a spike test at a multiple of it. Soak matters only if you expect days of sustained traffic.

### Choose a realistic target

You need an estimate of how many people arrive at once, drawn from your own evidence. Check your last broadcast: how many link clicks came in the first ten minutes, according to your email platform or link tracker? If you have never sent a campaign, start from the size of the list you will message and assume a meaningful share could open the link in the first hour. Treat this as a planning assumption, write it down, and run the spike test above it so you learn what happens past your estimate.

### A small k6 example

k6 scripts are JavaScript. Thresholds turn a test into pass or fail: the k6 documentation shows a minimal example that sets a limit on the failed-request rate and on 95th percentile response time, and says that when a threshold is not met, "the test finishes with a failed status" and k6 exits with a non-zero code ([Grafana k6, thresholds](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/thresholds/)). A sketch of the idea, with limits you set yourself:

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  stages: [
    { duration: '2m', target: 20 },
    { duration: '30s', target: 200 },
    { duration: '2m', target: 200 },
  ],
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<1500'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://your-staging-site.example/campaign/');
  sleep(1);
}
```

The numbers are placeholders, not recommendations; set limits a donor on a slow phone would tolerate. The k6 guidance on large tests advises keeping the load generator's own CPU use within 80 percent, so your test machine is not the bottleneck ([Grafana k6, running large tests](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/testing-guides/running-large-tests/)).

Other tools exist, including hosted services. The tool matters less than the discipline: a written scenario, a target, a pass mark and a record of the results.

### Where and how to test safely

- **Test a staging copy** hosted like production, so live donors are not at risk.
- **Get your host's permission.** Some providers treat a sudden flood as abuse and may block or suspend you; tell them the window or follow their load-testing policy.
- **Do not load test a live payment provider.** Use its test mode, and read its terms.
- **Test the whole journey:** campaign page, amount selection, order creation and thank-you page.
- **Repeat after changes** such as a new plugin, theme update or hosting plan.

Afterwards ask four things: at what number of simultaneous visitors did pages become too slow, which page produced errors, did the site recover when load fell, and what is the cheapest fix for the weakest link? Fix it, then test again.

## Monitor from outside, and decide who gets the alert

A test tells you about a rehearsal. Monitoring tells you about the real day. An uptime monitor checks your site at intervals from outside your hosting and alerts you when a check fails. For a campaign, monitor the campaign URL, the donation page and the thank-you page, plus SSL expiry. See [website uptime monitoring for business](/blog/website-uptime-monitoring-business), and read [how to choose a hosting uptime SLA](/blog/hosting-uptime-sla-for-business) before relying on a percentage on a plan page, since what counts as downtime differs between providers.

Three points for a spike day. Alerts must reach a human who can act: an inbox nobody reads at 9 pm is not an alert, so send it to two phones with a named person on call. And alert on slowness as well as outages, because a page that answers in twelve seconds is "up" and failing. If your host shows CPU and memory graphs, keep them open; they show whether to cache, upgrade or wait.

## A status page and an offline fallback

Assume that at some point something will fail, and design what the donor sees when it does. The worst outcome is a blank screen or a raw server error. A better outcome is a calm, honest page that tells people what to do.

### A status page hosted elsewhere

If your server is down, a page on that same server is down too. Keep a simple "we are busy" page on a different service, such as a static page on separate hosting, and know in advance how to switch to it: DNS changes take time to spread, and some CDN and hosting products can serve a custom error page when your origin is not responding, so check what yours offers. The page should say calmly that donations are welcome, that the site is under heavy load, what to do now and when to retry. Do not blame the donor or use technical language.

### Offline ways to give

Keep ready a short block you can paste anywhere: bank transfer details with account name, account number and IFSC, and a phone or WhatsApp number for help. Confirm the wording with your chartered accountant and finance team, check it against bank records before each campaign, and make sure offline donors know how to get an acknowledgement. Also write the messages you will send when the site is slow, and decide who checks a doubtful gift, such as a donor charged but without a receipt.

## Choosing hosting for a spike: a decision table

There is no single right answer, and prices change, so this table compares options in general terms. Read each provider's own documentation for specifics.

| Option | Strengths | Weak points for spikes | Usually suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic shared hosting | Lowest cost, simple | Per-account resource limits, little control over caching | A small informational site with small campaigns |
| Shared hosting plus CDN and page cache | Cheap improvement; offloads static files and cached pages | HTML cached only if configured; donation step still reaches your server | NGOs with occasional campaigns |
| Managed WordPress hosting | Server-level caching, WordPress-aware support | Plan limits still apply; read the visit allowances | Most WordPress NGO sites with seasonal campaigns |
| Cloud server (VPS) | Dedicated resources; scale up before a campaign | Someone must set up, secure and maintain it | NGOs with a developer or agency |
| Static campaign page on separate hosting or CDN, hosted payment step | Public page barely touches a server | Needs a clean hand-off to your donor records | High-visibility appeals that may go viral |
| Hosted donation platform | Provider manages scaling of the form | Less control; data and branding trade-offs | Teams without technical support |

Ask each provider in writing: what happens when I exceed my limits, how fast can I upgrade, what caching is included, what is your load-testing policy, and how do I reach support on a weekend or holiday? A temporary upgrade for the campaign window may beat permanent capacity you rarely use.

## The two-week pre-campaign checklist

Count back from launch day. With less time, do the early items and accept the remaining risk knowingly.

**Days 14 to 10**

- Name a technical owner and a weekend backup; list the pages that must work.
- Pick the hosting approach and confirm plan limits, upgrade options and support contacts in writing.
- Remove unused plugins, update on a staging copy, and take a backup you have tested restoring.
- Write down your traffic planning assumption and its source.

**Days 9 to 7**

- Turn on page caching for public pages and a CDN for static files; add an HTML rule only for pages identical for everyone.
- Check that the donation form, receipts and logged-in areas are excluded and still work.
- Check email and SMS limits; queue receipts instead of sending them inside the donation request.

**Days 6 to 4**

- Run smoke, load and spike tests against staging, using payment test mode only.
- Fix the weakest link, retest and record the results.

**Days 3 to 2**

- Set up uptime monitoring on the campaign, donation and thank-you pages; confirm alerts reach two phones.
- Prepare and rehearse the off-server status page and the finance-approved offline giving text.
- Check SSL and domain expiry dates.

**Day 1 and launch day**

- Freeze changes: no plugin or theme updates until the campaign ends.
- Confirm the on-call person, your host's escalation contact and the rule for switching to the status page.
- Stagger broadcasts (email first, WhatsApp later) so the first minutes are less abrupt.
- Afterwards, review monitoring logs and support messages, and return to your normal plan.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do I know if my NGO website can handle a sudden surge of donors?

Test it. Run a spike test, with a tool such as k6, against a staging copy of your site, using the payment provider's test mode, and see at what number of simultaneous visitors pages slow down or fail. Without a test, a surge on your hosting plan is guesswork.

### Does using Cloudflare or another CDN protect my donation page from a traffic spike?

It helps, but not automatically. Cloudflare's documentation says its CDN does not cache HTML or JSON by default, so your page still comes from your server until you create a rule for it. Cache only public pages that are the same for everyone, and keep donation forms and receipts out of the cache.

### Is shared hosting enough for a campaign?

Sometimes, for a small appeal, especially with page caching and a CDN in front. Shared plans have per-account resource limits, so ask your host what happens when you exceed them, and consider a temporary upgrade or a static campaign page for appeals that could go viral.

### What should a donor see if the site goes down during a campaign?

A plain, calm status page hosted somewhere other than your main server, saying that donations are welcome, what to do now and when to retry, plus your approved offline giving instructions and a contact number. Prepare it and practise the switch before launch day.

### How long before a campaign should we prepare for traffic?

Two weeks gives time to fix hosting and caching, run tests, set up monitoring and prepare fallbacks. With less, prioritise page caching for the campaign page, a basic test, uptime alerts to two phones and a status page, and accept the remaining risk knowingly.
